messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
The test `testPcts()` is failing possibly because of a mismatch between the actual and expected results of the method `getPct(Object)`.

From the current bug report, `getPct(Object v)` is deprecated and internally calls `getCumPct((Comparable<?>) v)`. This means it actually returns a cumulative percentage, rather than just the percentage for that specific value.

The code confirms this:
- `getPct(Object v)` (deprecated) calls `getCumPct((Comparable<?>) v)`.
- `getPct(Comparable<?> v)` returns the percentage of occurrences of the specific value `v`.
- `getCumPct(Comparable<?> v)` returns the cumulative percentage of all values less than or equal to `v`.

The failing test `testPcts()` asserts that the percentage for the value "three" is 0.5 using `getPct((Object) Integer.valueOf(3))`. Because this calls the deprecated `getPct(Object)`, which returns the cumulative percentage instead of the exact percentage, the test would fail.

The root cause is that `getPct(Object)` is deprecated but still used in the test, resulting in the use of cumulative percentage (`getCumPct`) instead of the intended `getPct(Comparable)`.

The recent bug reports do not add relevant information.

The correct fix involves updating the calls to `getPct(Object)` (deprecated method) to use `getPct(Comparable<?>)` instead, or removing usage of the deprecated method to prevent confusion and ensure proper percentage retrieval.

Summary:
- Deprecated `getPct(Object)` used in test returns cumulative percentage instead of exact.
- Test expects exact percentage but receives cumulative due to deprecated method.
- Method `getPct(Comparable<?>)` provides correct exact percentage.
- Fix requires avoiding the deprecated method in favor of the `Comparable` variant.

This diagnosis explains the failure of `testPcts()` and aligns with the current bug report.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
